Currency value isn't actually based on anything. Not in real terms. Currency is valued by the international market by how much it costs to buy and sell that currency, just as with stocks, shares, bonds, etc, etc. That was the whole point of Nixon abandoning Bretton Woods in 1971: the US was the last world power that still pegged the value of its fiat currency to a fixed quantity of gold. The downside of gold prices for currency is that you can't expand the money supply without finding more gold, which is exceedingly rare: in all human history we've only mined a very small quantity of it, comparatively speaking.

But a country certainly can print money based on nothing. It's just a matter of how long before anyone notices and how long before the market takes notice and accordingly ditches that currency as holding no value. The US only gets away with it -- via quantitative easing, which might not be called printing money but certainly is in real terms -- because every other currency on the face of the planet is a piece of inflated, unstable shit or doesn't have sufficient volume to be the world's reserve currency. When one of those factors changes -- or for some reason the market at large becomes convinced the US will never in fact pay off its debts, which amounts to the same as a promise that the money of the US is or will soon be worthless -- hyperinflation hits.
